Let \(g\geq2\) be an integer, and set
\[
r=\left\lfloor\frac{g+2}{3}\right\rfloor,\qquad k=g-r.
\]
Let \(C_g\) be the smooth projective completion over \(\mathbb C\) of the affine curve
\[
z^2=x^{2g+1}-1,
\]
and let \(p\) be its unique point over infinity. Choose the local parameter \(t\) at \(p\) satisfying
\[
x=t^{-2},\qquad z=t^{-(2g+1)}(1-t^{4g+2})^{1/2},
\]
where the square root has value \(1\) at \(t=0\).

For a nonzero vector \(b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{r-1})\in\mathbb C^r\), define
\[
\phi_b(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}b_jt^{-(2g-1-2j)}.
\]
Choose coordinate discs \(W_0\Subset W\) centered at \(p\), with \(t\) defined on a neighborhood of \(\overline W\), and put \(U=C_g\setminus\overline{W_0}\). Take product neighborhoods of the zero sections over \(U\) and \(W\), with fiber coordinates \(y_U\) and \(y_W\). After shrinking the fiber directions, glue them over \(U\cap W\), preserving the base point, by
\[
y_W=t^{-1}y_U\bigl(1+k\phi_b(t)y_U^k\bigr)^{-1/k}.
\]
The fractional power denotes the holomorphic branch whose value is \(1\) at \(y_U=0\).

Let \(X_b\) be the resulting smooth analytic surface germ along its zero section \(E\simeq C_g\). Its normal bundle is \(\mathcal O_{C_g}(-p)\), and contracting \(E\) gives a normal surface singularity \((V_b,0)\) with minimal good resolution \(f_b:(X_b,E)\to(V_b,0)\). For cohomology, take \(X_b\) to be the inverse image of a sufficiently small Stein representative of this singularity.

Write \(\mathcal I_E\) for the ideal sheaf of \(E\), and define the logarithmic tangent sheaf by
\[
S_b=\{D\in\Theta_{X_b}:D(\mathcal I_E)\subseteq\mathcal I_E\},
\]
where \(\Theta_{X_b}\) is the sheaf of holomorphic vector fields. Put \(L_b=\bigwedge^2S_b\) and \(h^1(X_b,\mathcal F)=\dim_{\mathbb C}H^1(X_b,\mathcal F)\). Determine the exact formula, as a function of \(g\) and the entire coefficient vector \(b\), for
\[
\Delta_b=h^1(X_b,\mathcal O_{X_b})-h^1(X_b,S_b)+h^1(X_b,L_b),
\]
for every allowed nonzero \(b\), including vectors with vanishing components.
</problem>

148	## 3. Derivation of the transition matrices
149	
150	Put \(u=y_U\), \(w=y_W\), and
151	\[
152	H=1-k\phi t^k w^k.
153	\]
154	The inverse fiber change is
155	\[
156	u=twH^{-1/k}.                                                    \tag{11}
157	\]
158	On \(C_g\setminus\{p\}\), use the nowhere-zero vector field
159	\[
160	\delta=z\partial_x+\frac{2g+1}{2}x^{2g}\partial_z.
161	\]
162	Near \(p\),
163	\[
164	\delta=a\partial_t.
165	\]
166	Use logarithmic vertical frames
167	\(\eta_U=u\partial_u\) and \(\eta_W=w\partial_w\). Direct differentiation gives
168	\[
169	\begin{split}
170	\eta_U&=H\eta_W,\\
171	\delta_U&=
172	a\partial_t+
173	a\left(-t^{-1}-t^k\phi'w^k\right)\eta_W,\\
174	\delta_U\wedge\eta_U&=aH\,\partial_t\wedge\eta_W.                 \tag{12}
175	\end{split}
176	\]
177	Also,
178	\[
179	u^n=t^nw^nH^{-n/k}.
180	\]
181	Expanding the powers of \(H\), and retaining fiber degrees at most \(N\), gives exactly (2). In particular the off-diagonal term of \(T_S\), including the \(\phi'\)-term, is necessary.

183	## 4. Why the finite matrices compute all global sections
184	
185	We give uniform bounds, so this argument never divides by any \(b_j\).
186	
187	The pole orders of \(\phi,\psi,t^k\phi'\) are at most \(q,d,d+1\), respectively. Every entry of the matrices \(T_O,T_S,T_L\) consequently has valuation at least
188	\[
189	-P=-Jd-h-1.                                                      \tag{13}
190	\]
191	
192	We also need a bound for their inverses. In \(u\)-coordinates put
193	\[
194	Q=1+k\phi u^k.
195	\]
196	The inverse versions of (11)–(12) are
197	\[
198	\begin{split}
199	w^n&=t^{-n}u^nQ^{-n/k},\\
200	\eta_W&=Q\eta_U,\\
201	\partial_t\big|_w
202	 &=a^{-1}\delta_U+
203	 \left[t^{-1}+\left(\phi'+\frac{k\phi}{t}\right)u^k\right]\eta_U.
204	                                                                    \tag{14}
205	\end{split}
206	\]
207	A coefficient involving \(\ell\) fiber-degree increments has valuation at least
208	\[
209	-n-\ell q-1.
210	\]
211	Since \(n+\ell k\leq N\),
212	\[
213	n+\ell q+1
214	=(n+\ell k)+\ell d+1\leq N+Jd+1=M.
215	\]
216	Thus every inverse-transition entry has valuation at least \(-M\).
217	
218	Let a global section of one of \(O_N,S_N,L_N\) have coefficient vector \(v\) in the \(U\)-frame. Its \(W\)-coefficient vector is holomorphic. The inverse-transition bound shows that every component of \(v\) is meromorphic at \(p\), with pole order at most \(M\).
219	
220	The meromorphic functions on \(C_g\) regular away from \(p\) form
221	\[
222	\mathbb C[x,z]/(z^2-x^{2g+1}+1).
223	\]
224	A basis for its subspace of pole order at most \(M\) is
225	\[
226	x^i\quad(2i\leq M),\qquad
227	zx^i\quad(2g+1+2i\leq M).
228	\]
229	Their expansions are precisely the \(f_\lambda\) used in (3).
230	
231	Consequently every possible global section is obtained by choosing a linear combination of these functions in every \(U\)-component and requiring that its transformed coefficients have no negative powers of \(t\). By (13), no negative exponent below \(-P-M\) can occur. Those conditions are exactly the linear equations (3).

233	Let

235	C=(N+1)|\Lambda_M|,
236	\qquad
237	\rho_O=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal B_O,\quad
238	\rho_S=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal B_S,\quad
239	\rho_L=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal B_L .

243	h^0(O_N)=C-\rho_O,\quad
244	h^0(S_N)=2C-\rho_S,\quad
245	h^0(L_N)=C-\rho_L.                                               \tag{15}

254	h^1(L)&=C-\rho_L-\chi(L_N).

181	## 4. Why the finite matrices compute all global sections
182	
183	We give uniform bounds, so this argument never divides by any \(b_j\).
184	
185	The pole orders of \(\phi,\psi,t^k\phi'\) are at most \(q,d,d+1\), respectively. Every entry of the matrices \(T_O,T_S,T_L\) consequently has valuation at least

190	We also need a bound for their inverses. In \(u\)-coordinates put
191	\[
192	Q=1+k\phi u^k.

195	\[
196	\begin{split}

198	\eta_W&=Q\eta_U,\\
199	\partial_t\big|_w

201	 \left[t^{-1}+\left(\phi'+\frac{k\phi}{t}\right)u^k\right]\eta_U.

206	\[

208	\]

223	\[
224	x^i\quad(2i\leq M),\qquad
225	zx^i\quad(2g+1+2i\leq M).
226	\]
